section.heading: 1.8 Introduction to Linear Transformations
section.paragraph: The difference between a matrix equation $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ and the associated vector equation $$x_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1} + \cdots + x_{n}\mathbf{a}_{n} = \mathbf{b}$$ is merely a matter of notation. However, a matrix equation $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ can arise in linear algebra (and in applications such as computer graphics and signal processing) in a way that is not directly connected with linear combinations of vectors. This happens when we think of the matrix $$A$$ as an object that “acts” on a vector $$\mathbf{x}$$ by multiplication to produce a new vector called $$A\mathbf{x}$$ .
For instance, the equations

$$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}4 & - 3 & & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 & & 5 & 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}5 \\ 8\end{matrix} \left]\right. & \text{and} & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}4 & - 3 & & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 & & 5 & 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 4 \\ - 1 \\ 3\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}0 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. \uparrow & \uparrow & & \uparrow & & \uparrow & \uparrow & & \uparrow A & x & & b & & A & u & & 0$$
say that multiplication by $$A$$ transforms $$\mathbf{x}$$ into $$\mathbf{b}$$ and transforms $$\mathbf{u}$$ into the zero vector. See Figure 1.

image.alt: A figure shows the transformation of vectors via matrix multiplication with two vertical planes and arrows in between.

section.paragraph: Click here for an interactive version of Figure 1

From this new point of view, solving the equation $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ amounts to finding all vectors $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ that are transformed into the vector $$\mathbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ under the “action” of multiplication by $$A$$ .

The correspondence from $$\mathbf{x}$$ to $$A\mathbf{x}$$ is a function from one set of vectors to another. This concept generalizes the common notion of a function as a rule that transforms one real number into another.

A ﻿transformation (or function or mapping) $$T$$ from $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ to $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ is a rule that assigns to each vector $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ a vector $$T(\mathbf{x})$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ . The set $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is called the domain of $$T$$ , and $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ is called the codomain of $$T$$ . The notation $$T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ indicates that the domain of $$T$$ is $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and the codomain is $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ . For $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , the vector $$T(\mathbf{x})$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ is called the image of $$\mathbf{x}$$ (under the action of $$T$$ ). The set of all images $$T(\mathbf{x})$$ is called the range of $$T$$ . See Figure 2.

The new terminology in this section is important because a dynamic view of matrix–vector multiplication is the key to understanding several ideas in linear algebra and to building mathematical models of physical systems that evolve over time. Such dynamical systems will be discussed in Sections 1.10, 4.8, and throughout Chapter 5.
section.heading: Matrix Transformations
section.paragraph: The rest of this section focuses on mappings associated with matrix multiplication. For each $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , $$T(\mathbf{x})$$ is computed as $$A\mathbf{x}$$ , where $$A$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix. For simplicity, we sometimes denote such a matrix transformation by $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$$ . Observe that the domain of $$T$$ is $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ when $$A$$ has $$n$$ columns and the codomain of $$T$$ is $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ when each column of $$A$$ has $$m$$ entries. The range of $$T$$ is the set of all linear combinations of the columns of $$A$$ , because each image $$T(\mathbf{x})$$ is of the form $$A\mathbf{x}$$ .

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & {- 3} \\ 3 & 5 \\ {- 1} & 7 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{b} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 2 \\ {- 5} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{c} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and define a transformation $$T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ by $$T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$$ , so that

$$T ( \mathbf{x} ) = A \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 \\ 3 & 5 \\ - 1 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} - 3 x_{2} \\ 3 x_{1} + 5 x_{2} \\ - x_{1} + 7 x_{2} \end{bmatrix}$$

list.item: Find $$T(\mathbf{u})$$ , the image of $$\mathbf{u}$$ under the transformation $$T$$ .
Find an $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ whose image under $$T$$ is $$\mathbf{b}$$ .
Is there more than one $$\mathbf{x}$$ whose image under $$T$$ is $$\mathbf{b} ?$$
Determine if $$\mathbf{c}$$ is in the range of the transformation $$T$$ .

image.alt: A figure shows the conversion of the two-dimensional graph to a three-dimensional graph indicated by an arrow T.

example.heading: Solution

list.item: Solve $$T(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{b}$$ for $$\mathbf{x}$$ . That is, solve $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ , or

example.paragraph: $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 \\ 3 & 5 \\ - 1 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ - 5 \end{bmatrix}$$

list.item: Using the method discussed in Section 1.4, row reduce the augmented matrix:

example.paragraph: $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & 2 \\ - 1 & 7 & - 5 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 14 & - 7 \\ 0 & 4 & - 2 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & - . 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1.5 \\ 0 & 1 & - . 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

list.item: Hence $$x_{1} = 1.5$$ , $$x_{2} = - .5$$ , and $$\mathbf{x} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1.5 \\ {- .5} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . The image of this $$\mathbf{x}$$ under $$T$$ is the given vector $$\mathbf{b}$$ .

Any $$\mathbf{x}$$ whose image under $$T$$ is $$\mathbf{b}$$ must satisfy equation (1). From (2), it is clear that equation (1) has a unique solution. So there is exactly one $$\mathbf{x}$$ whose image is $$\mathbf{b}$$ .

The vector $$\mathbf{c}$$ is in the range of $$T$$ if $$\mathbf{c}$$ is the image of some $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ , that is, if $$\mathbf{c} = T(\mathbf{x})$$ for some $$\mathbf{x}$$ . This is just another way of asking if the system $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{c}$$ is consistent. To find the answer, row reduce the augmented matrix: $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & 2 \\ - 1 & 7 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 14 & - 7 \\ 0 & 4 & 8 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 14 & - 7 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & - 35 \end{bmatrix}$$ The third equation, $$0 = - 35$$ , shows that the system is inconsistent. So $$\mathbf{c}$$ is not in the range of $$T$$ .

section.paragraph: The question in Example 1(c) is a uniqueness problem for a system of linear equations, translated here into the language of matrix transformations: Is $$\mathbf{b}$$ the image of a unique $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n} \text{?}$$ Similarly, Example 1(d) is an existence problem: Does there exist an $$\mathbf{x}$$ whose image is $$\mathbf{c} ?$$

The next two matrix transformations can be viewed geometrically. They reinforce the dynamic view of a matrix as something that transforms vectors into other vectors. Section 2.7 contains other interesting examples connected with computer graphics.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: If $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ , then the transformation $$\mathbf{x} \rightarrowtail A \mathbf{x}$$ projects points in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ onto the $$x_{1}x_{2} \text{-plane}$$ because

$$\begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3} \end{bmatrix} \rightarrowtail \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$
See Figure 3.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . The transformation $$\mathbf{T}:\mathbb{R}^{ \text{2} }\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ defined by $$T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$$ is called a shear transformation. It can be shown that if $$T$$ acts on each point in the $$2 \times 2$$ square shown in Figure 4, then the set of images forms the sheared parallelogram. The key idea is to show that $$T$$ maps line segments onto line segments (as shown in Exercise 35) and then to check that the corners of the square map onto the vertices of the parallelogram. For instance, the image of the point $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ is $$T(\mathbf{u}) = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 4 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and the image of $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ is $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 6 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . $$T$$ deforms the square as if the top of the square were pushed to the right while the base is held fixed. Shear transformations appear in physics, geology, and crystallography.

section.heading: Linear Transformations
section.paragraph: Theorem 5 in Section 1.4 shows that if $$A$$ is $$m \times n$$ , then the transformation $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$$ has the properties
$$A \left(\right. \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \left.\right) = A \mathbf{u} + A \mathbf{v} \text{and} A \left(\right. c \mathbf{u} \left.\right) = c A \mathbf{u}$$

for all $$\mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and all scalars $$c$$ . These properties, written in function notation, identify the most important class of transformations in linear algebra.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A transformation (or mapping) $$T$$ is linear if

list.item: $$T(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = T(\mathbf{u}) + T(\mathbf{v})$$ for all $$\mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v}$$ in the domain of $$T$$ ;
$$T(c\mathbf{u}) = cT(\mathbf{u})$$ for all scalars $$c$$ and all $$\mathbf{u}$$ in the domain of $$T$$ .

section.paragraph: Every matrix transformation is a linear transformation. Important examples of linear transformations that are not matrix transformations will be discussed in Chapters 4 and 5.

Linear transformations preserve the operations of vector addition and scalar multiplication. Property (i) says that the result $$T(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v})$$ of first adding $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and then applying $$T$$ is the same as first applying $$T$$ to $$\mathbf{u}$$ and to $$\mathbf{v}$$ and then adding $$T(\mathbf{u})$$ and $$T(\mathbf{v})$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ . These two properties lead easily to the following useful facts.

note.paragraph: If $$T$$ is a linear transformation, then
$$T \left(\right. c \mathbf{u} + d \mathbf{v} \left.\right) = c T \left(\right. \mathbf{u} \left.\right) + d T \left(\right. \mathbf{v} \left.\right)$$
for all vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ in the domain of $$T$$ and all scalars $$c \text{,} d$$ .

section.paragraph: Property (3) follows from condition (ii) in the definition, because $$T(0) = T(0\mathbf{u}) = 0T(\mathbf{u}) = 0$$ . Property (4) requires both (i) and (ii):

$$T \left(\right. c \mathbf{u} + d \mathbf{v} \left.\right) = T \left(\right. c \mathbf{u} \left.\right) + T \left(\right. d \mathbf{v} \left.\right) = c T \left(\right. \mathbf{u} \left.\right) + d T \left(\right. \mathbf{v} \left.\right)$$

Observe that if a transformation satisfies (4) for all $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ and $$c$$ , $$d$$ , it must be linear. (Set $$c = d = 1$$ for preservation of addition, and set $$d = 0$$ for preservation of scalar multiplication.) Repeated application of (4) produces a useful generalization:
$$\boxed{T ( c_{1} \mathbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} \mathbf{v}_{p} ) = c_{1} T ( \mathbf{v}_{1} ) + \hdots + c_{p} T ( \mathbf{v}_{p} )}$$

In engineering and physics, (5) is referred to as a superposition principle. Think of $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p}$$ as signals that go into a system and $$T(\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{),…,} T(\mathbf{v}_{p})$$ as the responses of that system to the signals. The system satisfies the superposition principle if whenever an input is expressed as a linear combination of such signals, the system’s response is the same linear combination of the responses to the individual signals. We will return to this idea in Chapter 4.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Given a scalar $$r$$ , define $$T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ by $$T(\mathbf{x}) = r\mathbf{x}$$ . $$T$$ is called a contraction when $$0 \leq r \leq 1$$ and a dilation when $$r > 1$$ . Let $$r = 3$$ , and show that $$T$$ is a linear transformation.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Let $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ be in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ and let $$c$$ , $$d$$ be scalars. Then

$$T \left(\right. c \mathbf{u} + d \mathbf{v} \left.\right) & = 3 \left(\right. c \mathbf{u} + d \mathbf{v} \left.\right) & \text{Definition} \text{of} T & \begin{matrix}= 3 c \mathbf{u} + 3 d \mathbf{v} \\ = c \left(\right. 3 \mathbf{u} \left.\right) + d \left(\right. 3 \mathbf{v} \left.\right)\end{matrix} \left.\right} & \text{Vector} \text{arithmetic} & = c T \left(\right. \mathbf{u} \left.\right) + d T \left(\right. \mathbf{v} \left.\right) &$$
Thus $$T$$ is a linear transformation because it satisfies (4). See Figure 5.

image.alt: Two graphs show a dilation transformation of five vectors by an arrow T.

example.paragraph: Click here to see an interactive example of dilation and contraction

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Define a linear transformation $$T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ by
$$T ( \mathbf{x} ) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & - 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} - x_{2} \\ x_{1} \end{bmatrix}$$

Find the images under $$T$$ of $$\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and $$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: $$T \left(\right. \mathbf{u} \left.\right) = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}0 & - 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}4 \\ 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ 4\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , T \left(\right. \mathbf{v} \left.\right) = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}0 & - 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}2 \\ 3\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 3 \\ 2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , T \left(\right. \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \left.\right) = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}0 & - 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}6 \\ 4\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 4 \\ 6\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$

Note that $$T(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v})$$ is obviously equal to $$T(\mathbf{u}) + T(\mathbf{v})$$ . It appears from Figure 6 that $$T$$ rotates $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ , and $$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}$$ counterclockwise about the origin through $$90{^\circ}$$ . In fact, $$T$$ transforms the entire parallelogram determined by $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ into the one determined by $$T(\mathbf{u})$$ and $$T(\mathbf{v})$$ . (See Exercise 36.)

image.alt: A graph shows rotational transformation with a parallelogram in the first quadrant mirrored by another parallelogram in the second quadrant.

section.paragraph: The final example is not geometrical; instead, it shows how a linear mapping can transform one type of data into another.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: A company manufactures two products, $$\text{B}$$ and $$\text{C}$$ . Using data from Example 7 in Section 1.3, we construct a “unit cost” matrix, $$U = \lbrack\mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}\rbrack$$ , whose columns describe the “costs per dollar of output” for the products:

$$\text{Product} \begin{matrix} \text{B} & \text{C} \end{matrix} U = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.45 & .40 \\ .25 & .30 \\ .15 & .15\end{matrix} \left]\right. \begin{matrix} \text{Materials} \\ \text{Labor} \\ \text{Overhead} \end{matrix}$$

Let $$\mathbf{x} = \left( x_{1} \text{,} x_{2} \right)$$ be a “production” vector, corresponding to $$x_{1}$$ dollars of product $$\text{B}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ dollars of product $$\text{C}$$ , and define $$T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ by

$$T \left(\right. \mathbf{x} \left.\right) = U \mathbf{x} = x_{1} \left[\right. .45 .25 .15 \left]\right. + x_{2} \left[\right. .40 .30 .15 \left]\right. = \left[\right. \text{Total cost of materials} \text{Total cost of labor} \text{Total cost of overhead} \left]\right.$$
The mapping $$T$$ transforms a list of production quantities (measured in dollars) into a list of total costs. The linearity of this mapping is reflected in two ways:

list.item: If production is increased by a factor of, say, $$4$$ , from $$\mathbf{x}$$ to $$4\mathbf{x}$$ , then the costs will increase by the same factor, from $$T(\mathbf{x})$$ to $$4T(\mathbf{x})$$ .

If $$\mathbf{x}$$ and $$\mathbf{y}$$ are production vectors, then the total cost vector associated with the combined production $$\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}$$ is precisely the sum of the cost vectors $$T(\mathbf{x})$$ and $$T(\mathbf{y})$$ .

Suppose $$T:\mathbb{R}^{5}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ and $$T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$$ for some matrix $$A$$ and for each $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{5}$$ . How many rows and columns does $$A$$ have?
Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Give a geometric description of the transformation $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$$ .

The line segment from $$0$$ to a vector $$\mathbf{u}$$ is the set of points of the form $$t\mathbf{u}$$ , where $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ . Show that a linear transformation $$T$$ maps this segment into the segment between $$0$$ and $$T(\mathbf{u})$$ .
